Where it began

Matt Henry was born in Christchurch on 14 December 1991. He went to St Joseph's School in Papanui and then St Bede's College in the same city, and finished his school years on the other side of the world, with a one-year scholarship to St Joseph's College in Ipswich, England.

Back home he made his first-class debut for Canterbury in March 2011, in a Plunket Shield game against Wellington, and Canterbury stayed his home side from then on.

The player

He bowled right-arm fast-medium, and New Zealand first picked him in January 2014, for a one-day international against India. His Test debut followed on the tour of England in May 2015. Between then and 2026 he played 35 Tests and took 152 wickets at 26.05, with eight five-wicket hauls and one ten-wicket match. His best, 7 for 23, came against South Africa in February 2022, and it was his first Test five-for, which is quite a way to open the account.

He was part of the side that won the World Test Championship of 2019–2021, and of the team that beat India 3–0 in India in 2024. In white-ball cricket he took the wickets of David Warner and Michael Clarke in the 2015 World Cup final, was player of the match in the 2019 World Cup semi-final win over India with 3 for 37, and in April 2023 became the fourth New Zealander to take a T20 international hat-trick.

What made him special

Henry was a bowler for the big occasion. A World Cup final, a World Cup semi-final, a domestic T20 final and a world title in Tests all bear his fingerprints, and he took wickets in every format. When he got it going in English conditions he could be devastating: for Kent against Durham in April 2018 he took 12 for 73 in the match, his first ten-wicket haul.

With the bat he was handy down the order. He made 676 Test runs and four fifties, with a top score of 72, though a Test hundred never quite came. In a one-day game against India in 2016 he did add 84 with Jimmy Neesham for the ninth wicket, which as of March 2018 was a New Zealand record in one-day internationals.

Away from the middle

County cricket kept calling him back. He turned out for Worcestershire, Derbyshire and Kent, who gave him his county cap, and later Somerset. In 2023 he was the leading wicket-taker in England's T20 competition and took the final wicket against Essex to bring Somerset their first T20 title since 2005. He also played in the IPL, The Hundred and Major League Cricket.

And finally

He was not in New Zealand's original squad for the 2015 World Cup. He came in as a replacement, played in the semi-final and then took two wickets in the final at Melbourne. Not a bad tournament for a man who had missed the first cut.
